pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Balanced & Unbalanced Forces

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Lower KS2 Working Scientifically):** Setting up simple practical enquiries and comparative/fair tests; making systematic and careful observations and, where appropriate, taking accurate measurements; the underlying balanced/unbalanced-force content sits in Year 5 Forces.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-PS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1] (assessment is qualitative and relative, one variable — number, size or direction — at a time, with gravity addressed as a downward pull).

- **Operational details:** This is a working-scientifically (procedural) topic mapped almost verbatim to NGSS 3-PS2-1: children PLAN and CONDUCT a fair-test investigation that provides evidence of how balanced and unbalanced forces affect an object's motion. The procedural core is variable control — change ONE variable (the number, size, or direction of forces) while keeping everything else the same — together with considering the NUMBER OF TRIALS (repeating readings). At 8-9 the force science stays qualitative and relative (bigger/smaller push, not measured newtons) and gravity is treated simply as a downward pull. The concept under the procedure: balanced forces (equal in size, opposite in direction) produce no change in motion; unbalanced forces change motion. Canonical contexts are tug-of-war (isolate force strength), motion across different surfaces (friction), and parachute canopy area.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Frame the investigation around ONE testable question with a single independent variable (e.g. does a bigger push on one side change the motion?) and control the rest
Explicitly teach the two markers of a fair test — control variables AND consider the number of trials (repeat readings) — not just the slogan 'fair test' (NGSS SEP; Oak)
Model an investigation first, then release pupils to design their own (gradual release)
Require pupils to use their RESULTS as evidence to decide balanced vs unbalanced, rather than asserting the answer in advance
Keep it qualitative and relative at this age (no force measurement); treat gravity as a downward pull (NGSS assessment boundary)
Use tug-of-war as the canonical balanced↔unbalanced context; surface-friction and parachute area as alternatives; make predictions evidence-based, expecting trend-based reasoning
keyRepresentations: Fair-test planning frame / variable table: change one · measure · keep the same
Force-arrow diagram on the object — equal opposite arrows (balanced) vs unequal arrows giving a resultant (unbalanced)
Tug-of-war setup with a results table showing repeated trials
commonMisconceptions: 'Balanced forces' means there are NO forces / nothing is acting (balanced means equal and opposite, not absent)
Over-defaulting to 'fair test' as a slogan without grasping WHY only one variable may change (AKSIS: fair tests dominate primary practicals)
Changing more than one variable at once, or not repeating readings
Treating a prediction as a guess rather than reasoning from prior knowledge/evidence
The 'motion implies force' backbone — a moving object is thought to carry a force in its direction of travel
If a parachute/air-resistance context is used: that all objects experience the same air resistance regardless of size or shape

learn.summary: Procedural goal for 8–9 year-olds: plan and conduct a fair-test investigation that provides evidence of how balanced and unbalanced forces affect an object's motion. The craft is variable control (change exactly one of force number/size/direction, hold the rest constant), repeating readings, and then reading messy results to decide when forces are balanced (equal, opposite, no change in motion) versus unbalanced (motion changes). Science stays qualitative and relative (bigger/smaller pushes, not measured newtons); gravity is treated simply as a downward pull. The core experience should be a real hands-on investigation; a virtual investigation bench teaches the variable-control logic and is a strong complement but does not replace physically handling apparatus and real data.

activities.title: Run a real fair-test tug: how does the size of the pull change the motion?
feedback: If a learner labels the setup 'unbalanced' the instant any pull is applied while the trolley is still not moving: point out the trolley isn't moving, so the pull is being balanced by friction (or the held string) — that is balanced; unbalanced is when the motion CHANGES.

If a learner insists a steadily rolling trolley must have unbalanced forces: don't overload at this age — note that steady, unchanging motion is also balanced, and the constant-velocity case is deepened later.

If a learner changes two things at once (e.g. adds pulling mass AND swaps in a heavier trolley): rebuild so only the pulling force varies; ask 'which one caused the change?' so the need for one variable is felt.

If a learner treats balanced/unbalanced as separate memorised facts ('balanced = still, unbalanced = moving'): return them to their own trial — a still trolley with the pull cancelled = balanced; motion changing = unbalanced.
activities.rationale: The objective is procedural working-scientifically skill, so the learner must physically plan, run, repeat, and reason from real (messy) measurements rather than only recognise answers. Keeping it qualitative and relative matches the stated age expectation. The small-pull-held-still case is modelled with friction as an age-appropriate idealisation.
sourceClaims: The standard is to [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1], [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-3, 3-PS2-1, 5-PS1-4]; assessment is qualitative and relative (not quantitative force size), [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-1]), with gravity addressed as a downward pull.

A fair test is where only one variable is changed to see its effect; scientists control variables when planning fair tests; the working-scientifically skill is planning, carrying out and reviewing a fair-test investigation (in an air-resistance context).
learnerActions: Set up a wheeled trolley at rest on a table, a string over a pulley at the table edge, a small pot you can add identical masses to, plus a metre ruler and stopwatch.
Choose ONE thing to change — the size of the pulling force (add masses one at a time) — and list everything you will keep the same: same trolley, same surface, same starting point.
Predict, using what you already know, what will happen as the pull grows, and say why (reason from prior knowledge, not a blind guess).
Run each setting at least three times, recording distance travelled in a set time (or speed) in a results table.

Point to a moment when the trolley was NOT changing its motion (for example, a setting where the pull was too small to move it, if your data has one) and say what the forces were doing; point to a moment when the motion WAS changing (for example, the trolley speeding up after starting from rest).
Use your own data to conclude whether a bigger pulling force produces a bigger change in motion.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing only one variable and repeating readings lets you read results as evidence: if the trolley starts at rest and a small pull leaves it still, that pull is balanced by friction, so the forces are balanced (no change in motion); once the pull is bigger than the friction the forces become unbalanced and the trolley starts to move and speed up toward the pull, and a bigger unbalanced force makes a bigger change in motion.

activities.title: Virtual investigation bench: lock the variables and see why only one may change
feedback: If the learner changes more than one variable: the bench flags the confound and asks which change caused the effect, so the one-variable rule is experienced rather than recited.
If the learner says balanced means 'no forces at all': show the two equal arrows still present on the still cart — balanced means equal and opposite, not absent.
Live recolouring of the arrows and a results table that updates each trial can make the balanced↔unbalanced transition visible; offer these as optional supports, not required steps.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable model lets a learner isolate a variable, lock the rest, and observe the cause-effect of changing it, which supports control-of-variables reasoning. It is offered as a complement to real apparatus, not a substitute, because the hands-on enquiry craft is itself the goal; its comparative efficacy over other media is not established here.
sourceClaims: A fair test is where only one variable is changed to see its effect; scientists control variables when planning fair tests; the working-scientifically skill is planning, carrying out and reviewing a fair-test investigation (in an air-resistance context).
learnerActions: On a virtual tug-of-war or cart-with-pushers bench (cart starting at rest), pick ONE independent variable (e.g. the force on the left); the bench keeps the others the same by default (same cart, same surface, same number of pulls), though you can unlock them to test what happens if you change more than one.
Run the trial three times and watch a results table fill in; note that with equal, opposite forces the two arrows match and the cart stays still.
Nudge one force bigger and observe the cart, starting from rest, begin to move toward that force; connect the unequal arrows (a resultant) to the motion changing.
Deliberately try to change two things at once and respond to the bench's prompt ('you changed the surface AND the force; which one caused it?').
State from the table when forces were balanced (equal, opposite, no change in motion) and when unbalanced.
activities.intendedInsight: The variable-control logic can be experienced, not just stated: equal and opposite forces produce no change in motion; an unequal pair produces a resultant that changes motion (here, from rest, the cart starts moving toward the larger force); and changing two things at once makes the cause unreadable.

activities.title: Sort and sequence the fair-test reasoning (retrieval companion)
feedback: If a scenario with a still object under a small pull is marked unbalanced: remind that while motion is unchanging the forces cancel — balanced.
If only the slogan 'fair test' is given without naming the controlled variables: ask which specific things must be held the same and why.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, categorising and targeted questions can consolidate the procedural reasoning and vocabulary. This is a retrieval/consolidation aid: it checks and rehearses reasoning but does not itself elicit independent design and execution of an investigation, which the performance task must still provide.
learnerActions: Put the steps of a fair test in order: question with one variable → decide what to change, measure, and keep the same → run repeated trials → read results → conclude.
Categorise described scenarios as balanced (no change in motion) or unbalanced (motion changing), including a still object held by a small pull cancelled by friction.
Answer 'which variable should you change, and which must stay the same?' prompts for a given question.
Explain in a sentence why repeating readings matters.
activities.intendedInsight: Fair-test reasoning can be rehearsed: one variable changes, the rest are controlled, readings are repeated, and balanced/unbalanced is judged by whether motion changes.

activities.title: Labelled tug-of-war reference scene (vocabulary scaffold)
feedback: If the learner thinks the balanced state has no forces: point to the two equal arrows still shown — balanced means they cancel, not that they are gone.
Tap-to-reveal arrow states can make the contrast concrete; treat this as a reference, not a replacement for running trials.
activities.rationale: A fixed labelled scene supports vocabulary and set-up recognition. Because it is static it does not run trials or show the cause-effect of changing a variable, so it is a scaffold toward, not a substitute for, the live bench and the real investigation.
learnerActions: Study a labelled tug-of-war or cart scene; tap to reveal the force arrows in a balanced state (equal, opposite) and an unbalanced state (unequal, resultant).
Use a 'change one / keep the same' overlay to name the independent variable and the controlled variables for a chosen question.
Say aloud which state shows no change in motion and which shows motion changing.
activities.intendedInsight: Builds the set-up vocabulary and the look of balanced versus unbalanced force arrows before and alongside running a real test.

constraints: Keep the force science qualitative and relative at this age (bigger/smaller push, not measured newtons); treat gravity simply as a downward pull.

Balanced forces mean no CHANGE in motion (equal and opposite), which includes steady, unchanging motion — not necessarily being at rest. Avoid teaching 'balanced = still' as a rule; the constant-velocity case is deepened later.
Balanced does not mean no forces are acting; it means the forces cancel. A still object under a small pull cancelled by friction is balanced.

When a trolley starts at rest, an unbalanced pull makes it begin to move and speed up toward that pull; state the at-rest starting condition wherever 'speeds up' is claimed, and describe the resultant as changing motion rather than as the current direction of travel.
Change exactly one variable (number, size or direction of forces) and hold the rest constant; repeat readings to build the number-of-trials habit.

The learning objective is the hands-on enquiry craft: the performance task requires physically planning, running, repeating and reasoning from real data. The virtual bench, the sort/sequence companion, and the labelled scene are complements/scaffolds and do not on their own satisfy the procedural goal.
Recognition-only sorting and sequencing can rehearse and check reasoning but do not elicit independent design and execution of an investigation.
Treat predictions as evidence-based, trend-based reasoning from prior knowledge, not blind guesses.
The wheeled-trolley 'held still by friction under a small pull' is an age-appropriate simplification; present it qualitatively and do not over-formalise the friction mechanism at this age.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's '3D adds nothing' and 'static image cannot show cause-effect' claims and the 'only a live bench teaches the logic' framing were softened to scoped affordances/objective limits; catalog fit rankings and product/artefact-type labels were removed.

One source (AKSIS/PSTT enquiry guidance) was marked verified:false in the row. It directly backs the evidence-based/trend predictions and repeated-readings points and is retained only there; it was removed from the sort/sequence activity's sourceClaims because it does not support that activity's consolidation-via-sorting principle.

Self-audit of the force/motion logic: 'unbalanced when motion changes', 'balanced can include steady motion', 'a still trolley under a friction-cancelled pull is balanced', and 'from rest an unbalanced pull makes it start moving and speed up toward the pull' are internally consistent; 'balanced = stationary only' is treated as a misconception, not taught. No arithmetic or geometric claims required correction.

The friction model for a wheeled trolley held still under a small pull is an idealisation (rolling/axle resistance presented as friction); it is stated qualitatively in the activity and flagged here, not over-specified for the age group.

probeDeeper: Point to a time when the trolley wasn't changing its motion. What were the forces doing then?
What did you change, and what did you keep the same? Why does that matter?
When you added more mass to the pot, what happened — and does that make the forces more balanced or more unbalanced?
The trolley is sitting still with the string pulling gently. Balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: Changes only the pulling force (adds masses one at a time), keeps the trolley, surface and start point the same, and measures the effect on motion (distance in a set time, or speed), repeating readings. Reads the results as: while the trolley stays still and a small pull is cancelled by friction, the forces are balanced (no change in motion); once the pull is bigger than friction the forces are unbalanced and the trolley speeds up. Concludes a bigger unbalanced force makes a bigger change in motion.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'If a force is pulling it, the forces must be unbalanced — even before it moves.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point out the trolley isn't moving, so the pull is being cancelled (by friction / the held string) — that is balanced; unbalanced is when the motion CHANGES.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the setup unbalanced the moment a pull is applied, while the trolley is still not moving.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Balanced forces means the object has to be completely still — it can't be balanced if it's moving.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't overload at this age — note that steady, unchanging motion is also balanced, and deepen the constant-velocity case at KS3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists a trolley rolling steadily must have unbalanced forces.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'I'll add more pulling mass AND use a heavier trolley to make it interesting.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild so only the pulling force varies; keep the trolley and surface the same.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Changes two things between trials, so the motion changes for mixed reasons.

responseLevels.gap: Runs the setup but changes more than the force, or calls any situation with a force 'unbalanced'; can't connect results to balanced vs unbalanced.
responseLevels.full: Controls variables, measures the effect of force size with repeats, and reads the results relationally — identifies balanced (no change in motion, forces cancel) and unbalanced (motion changing, net force) moments in the actual trial and concludes a bigger unbalanced force makes a bigger change.
responseLevels.partial: Runs a fair-ish test and sees bigger pull -> more motion, and can define balanced and unbalanced, but treats them as separate facts ('balanced = still, unbalanced = moving') without reading their OWN moments — still trolley = pull cancelled = balanced; motion changing = unbalanced.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a wheeled trolley on the table, a string running over a pulley at the table's edge, a small pot you can add identical masses to, and a metre ruler and stopwatch. Plan and run a FAIR test to find out how the size of the pulling force changes how the trolley moves. Set it up, take your measurements, then use your results to point out a moment when the forces on the trolley were BALANCED and a moment when they were UNBALANCED.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because it is a procedure, you WATCH rather than ask about it. The discriminator is whether the child (a) controls variables so only force size changes and (b) reads 'no change in motion' as balanced and 'motion changing' as unbalanced. A child who labels the setup unbalanced the instant any pull is applied (even while it sits still), who thinks balanced means only-stationary, or who changes trolley mass and pull together, reveals the gap even if the measuring is fine.
